method: Today's real suite executions were read from the per-worktree test caches (<git-dir>/test-cache/*/stdout.txt, metadata.json) and cross-checked against the pi session tool-call durations (toolResult.durationMs for every run_tests.py / wait_for_job.py call), /var/log/llama-proxy/proxy.log and ss/top snapshots taken while the pool was saturated. No extra suite load was generated: the host was already carrying ~44 live agent sessions, so a synthetic F7 burst would only have distorted the measurement it measured.
caveat: Timing comes from pytest's own reported duration, so it excludes interpreter start-up and the runner's own overhead (<1 s per run). Suite duration is flat at both observed concurrency levels, which is the point: the pool was never compute-bound. Absolute latencies of the 1-3 s partial runs are taken from the pi session logs of the sessions that experienced them.

runs.note: early-day runs, nothing else in the pool
later runs while the pool was saturated

decision.rationale: Six concurrent suites cost at most six of thirty-two cores at the measured <1 core per suite, and leave 26 cores plus the GPU for the agent sessions that submit the work; four occupies the fast lane's burst peak without letting a storm of 1-3 s partial runs crowd out a finishing suite. The binding constraint was queue depth (97% pool utilisation at 92% host idle), so raising the ceiling and splitting the lanes attack the measured constraint rather than adding capacity nobody needed.
decision.residual_risk: A repo whose full suite is genuinely CPU-bound (e.g. a vitest/Chromium suite with an unbounded worker pool) must still set TEST_MAX_CONCURRENCY=1; the per-suite VITEST_MAX_WORKERS cap (default 4) remains in force for those.
